opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the biggest change is going to be in the length and complexity of tasks that models can carry out on their own. Right now, if you look at what these models are good at, it's mostly things you can do in one shot or over a few back-and-forth exchanges: answer a question, write a function, edit a document. What I expect over the next year or two is that they'll be able to handle much more involved projects. Instead of suggesting a function, you'd give it a high-level description, like "implement this feature" or "figure out why this test is failing and fix it," and it would go off, write code across a bunch of files, run it, look at the output, and iterate until it's done.

A lot of that comes from training models on longer-horizon tasks, where the reward depends on the whole trajectory and not just a single response. Once you train on that kind of data, I'd expect models to get much better at coherence over long stretches: keeping track of a goal, noticing when they've gone down the wrong path, and recovering from errors. Error recovery is a big piece of it. Right now models often get derailed. They make a mistake and either don't notice or compound it. Getting more robust there is less about raw intelligence and more about training them to be in that loop of acting, observing, and correcting.

I also think there's some sample efficiency at play. These models already know a lot from pretraining, so you may not need a huge amount of long-horizon training data to unlock a lot of capability. A relatively small amount of the right kind of data could teach the model to string together the skills it already has.

So my rough expectation is that we go from models that are like a helpful assistant you query, to something closer to a collaborator you can delegate a chunk of work to. That might be something that would take a person an hour, or eventually several hours. There will still be plenty of failure modes, but the trend toward longer, more autonomous tasks seems pretty clear to me.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that over the next year or two models will handle involved projects from high-level instructions, including writing code across files, running it, and iterating until the work is done.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing to watch is the length of tasks that models can do reliably. Right now, if you give a model something that takes a person a few minutes, it's usually fine. If you give it something that takes hours or days, it tends to go off the rails at some point. It makes a mistake, doesn't notice, and then compounds on that mistake, and eventually it's completely lost.

I think a lot of that comes down to a few things. One is just basic capability, like the model needs to be smart enough to do each step. But the bigger bottleneck is more about robustness and recovery. Can the model notice when something isn't working, back up, and try something else? Humans are pretty good at that. We hit a wall, we step back and reassess. Models historically haven't been trained to do much of that, because most of the training signal has been on short interactions where you give an answer and you're done.

So over the next year or two, I'd expect that to change a lot. People are now explicitly training models on longer-horizon tasks with RL, where the model actually has to take many actions in an environment, see the consequences, and get rewarded on the outcome. When you do that, the model starts to learn things like, "I should check my work," or "this approach isn't going anywhere, let me try something different." Those skills generalize surprisingly well.

My guess is that if you look at the horizon length that models can handle, it's been growing pretty steadily, maybe doubling every several months or so, and I don't see a reason for that to slow down soon. So in a year or two, you might have models that can take a fairly vague instruction, like "fix this bug" or "go figure out why this experiment isn't working," and just go work on it for hours or a day, come back with something reasonable. Not perfectly, you'll still have to check it, but a lot more like delegating to a junior colleague than like using a tool.

The other thing I'd expect is that the models get much better at handling the boring parts. A lot of what makes long tasks hard isn't the intellectually hard step, it's all the little things around it, setting up environments, figuring out the right file, remembering what you did three steps ago. Better context handling and better tool use will take care of a lot of that.

Where I'm less sure is how fast this gets adopted in practice. The capability can be there before the products and the trust are there. People need to figure out how to supervise these agents, how much to let them do on their own, what guardrails you want. I think that part is going to lag the raw capability by a while.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts models may handle vague tasks such as fixing a bug for hours or a day, but does not say they will autonomously complete entire coding projects from high-level instructions.

astra-6.text:
I expect them to get substantially better at tasks that require a long sequence of steps. There’s a gap right now between being able to answer a hard question and being able to work reliably for several hours toward some goal. A model might do each individual step reasonably well, but over a long task it makes a mistake, fails to notice it, and ends up going down the wrong path.

Over the next year or two, I think we’ll see progress in both the underlying capabilities and the ability to recover from mistakes—to check whether something worked, revise the plan, and keep going. Coding is a natural setting for that because you can run the code and get feedback.

I’m less sure how quickly that will translate into being able to hand off an entire project. Knowing when to ask for clarification, or recognizing that you’ve misunderstood what the user wants, can be as important as solving the technical problem. So I’d expect increasingly useful delegation, but with the amount of supervision depending a lot on the task and how easy it is to verify the result.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects better long-task performance and increasingly useful delegation, but says it is uncertain how quickly models will handle an entire project and expects supervision to vary. It does not predict autonomous completion of entire coding projects within one or two years.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect them to get substantially better at tasks that take a long time. Right now, a model can do something quite impressive in a short interaction, but if you ask it to work through a project with lots of steps, there are many opportunities for it to get confused or make a mistake that it doesn’t recover from. So reliability becomes a big bottleneck.

I think we’ll see progress in models being able to check their work, notice when an approach isn’t working, and try something else. That could make a pretty big difference in coding, for example, where you can run tests and get feedback along the way.

I’m less sure about how quickly that translates into being able to delegate an entire project. There’s a difference between solving a well-specified problem and figuring out what needs to be done, asking the right questions, and knowing when you’re finished. But over the next year or two, I’d expect the amount of work you can hand off without intervening to increase quite a bit.

r001.rationale: The response predicts more work can be handed off without intervention and discusses coding progress, but it does not predict that models will autonomously complete entire coding projects from high-level instructions. It explicitly expresses uncertainty about delegating an entire project.
